# Congruences and Saturation

The algebraic route to complementation partitions finite words into **finitely many classes**, then describes infinite words by products of classes. The whole idea rests on two everyday intuitions.

A **congruence** $\equiv$ on $\Sigma^{*}$ is an equivalence relation that is *respected by concatenation*: if $u\equiv u'$ and $w\equiv w'$ then $uw\equiv u'w'$. It has **finite index** if it has finitely many classes. The simplest non-trivial example — think even/odd — is **parity of length** over $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$:
$$ u \equiv_{\mathrm{par}} u' \iff |u|\equiv|u'| \pmod 2. $$
Two classes: `E` (even length, including $\varepsilon$) and `O` (odd length). The symbols read are irrelevant; only length parity matters.

A language $L$ is **saturated** by $\equiv$ if it is a *union of whole classes* — equivalently, $u\equiv u'$ never separates a member from a non-member. Saturation is exactly the property that lets us complement by flipping which classes we keep.

---

## Widget 1: classes and concatenation

Type two words. Each gets a class; their concatenation lands in the class predicted by the **class arithmetic** (E acts like $0$, O like $1$, modulo $2$) — never depending on *which* letters were used.

```{=html}
<div class="sc-lab" id="nb20a">
  <div class="input-row">
    <div class="input-group"><label>Word u</label><input type="text" id="nb20-u" value="a b a"></div>

<script>
(function(){
  const parse=s=>s.trim().split(/[\s,]+/).filter(x=>x.length);
  const cls=w=> w.length%2===0 ? 'E':'O';
  const chip=c=>`<span class="cls ${c}">${c}</span>`;
  function go(){
    const u=parse(document.getElementById('nb20-u').value), w=parse(document.getElementById('nb20-w').value);
    const uw=u.concat(w);
    const cu=cls(u),cw=cls(w),cuw=cls(uw);
    const ok = cuw === (( (u.length+w.length)%2===0)?'E':'O');
    document.getElementById('nb20-out').innerHTML=
      `u = "${u.join('')||'ε'}" &rarr; ${chip(cu)} (len ${u.length})<br>`+
      `w = "${w.join('')||'ε'}" &rarr; ${chip(cw)} (len ${w.length})<br>`+
      `uw = "${uw.join('')||'ε'}" &rarr; ${chip(cuw)} (len ${uw.length})<br><br>`+
      `class(uw) = ${chip(cu)} · ${chip(cw)} = ${chip(cuw)} &nbsp; ✓ predicted from the classes alone, not the letters.`;
  }
  document.getElementById('nb20-go').addEventListener('click',go);
  ['nb20-u','nb20-w'].forEach(id=>document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('keyup',e=>{if(e.key==='Enter')go();}));
  go();
})();
</script>
```

## Widget 2: is $L$ saturated?

A language is saturated iff every class lies **entirely inside** or **entirely outside** it. The widget probes each class with two representatives; if one is in $L$ and the other is not, the class is *split* and $L$ is **not** saturated by $\equiv_{\mathrm{par}}$.

```{=html}
<div class="sc-lab" id="nb20b">
  <div class="input-row">
    <div class="input-group" style="min-width:260px;">
      <label>Language L</label>
      <select id="nb20-lang">
        <option value="0">L = words of even length</option>
        <option value="1">L = words of odd length</option>
        <option value="2">L = words containing at least one a</option>
        <option value="3">L = words of length ≥ 3</option>
      </select>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="sc-panel" id="nb20-sat"></div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const cls=w=> w.length%2===0 ? 'E':'O';
  const chip=c=>`<span class="cls ${c}">${c}</span>`;
  const LANGS=[
    {name:'even length', test:w=>w.length%2===0},
    {name:'odd length', test:w=>w.length%2===1},
    {name:'contains an a', test:w=>w.includes('a')},
    {name:'length ≥ 3', test:w=>w.length>=3}
  ];
  // representatives per class E,O
  const reps={E:[[],['a','a'],['b','b'],['a','b']], O:[['a'],['b'],['a','a','a'],['b','a','b']]};
  function render(){
    const L=LANGS[+document.getElementById('nb20-lang').value];
    let html=''; let saturated=true; const rows=[];
    for(const c of ['E','O']){
      const results=reps[c].map(w=>({w,inL:L.test(w)}));
      const allIn=results.every(r=>r.inL), allOut=results.every(r=>!r.inL);
      const split=!(allIn||allOut); if(split) saturated=false;
      rows.push({c,results,split,verdict: allIn?'wholly IN':allOut?'wholly OUT':'SPLIT'});
    }
    html+=`<h4>Probing the two classes</h4>`;
    for(const r of rows){
      html+=`<div style="margin-bottom:8px;">${chip(r.c)} `+
        r.results.map(x=>`"${x.w.join('')||'ε'}"${x.inL?'&#8712;':'&#8713;'}L`).join(' &nbsp; ')+
        ` &rarr; <strong style="color:${r.split?'#c0392b':'#0f6b5c'}">${r.verdict}</strong></div>`;
    }
    html+=`<div class="verdict-box ${saturated?'verdict-pass':'verdict-fail'}">`+
      (saturated
        ? `<strong>Saturated.</strong> Each class is entirely in or entirely out, so L is a union of ≡par-classes. Complementing L is just flipping which classes we keep.`
        : `<strong>Not saturated.</strong> A class is split — ≡par is too coarse to describe L, because two words of the same length parity disagree on membership. A finer congruence would be needed.`)
      +`</div>`;
    document.getElementById('nb20-sat').innerHTML=html;
  }
  document.getElementById('nb20-lang').addEventListener('change',render);
  render();
})();
</script>
```

Parity is a toy congruence — it only saturates length-parity languages. The chapter's real congruence, $\approx_{\mathcal A}$, is much finer: it remembers *which states an automaton can traverse* on a word, and it saturates the language of any Büchi automaton. That is the subject of **[Notebook 21](21-approx-a-profile.qmd)**.
